note: Whole-step bends checked against the fretted note two frets up and a drone, vibrato on the held bend to the metronome, then both in a minor blues solo. One position is on the screen now, so it names no number; the key is moves (any key) and named only as {{=key}}, each block has one extra line, and the last says what stays the same in another key. missing: no tool listens to a bend or marks one in tab, so the drone and the player's ear do the checking.

exercise.title: Bends in tune, then vibrato
exercise.why: A whole-step bend is in tune when it sounds the same as the note two frets higher, so playing that fretted note first gives your ear the pitch to bend up to.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the drone on {{=key}}. Under it is the neck with the notes of the {{=key}} minor pentatonic scale, with {{4}} and {{5}} ringed. On the G string, play the ringed {{5}}, then bend the ringed {{4}} two frets under it until it sounds the same.
Push the string with three fingers behind each other, and stop the bend where the two notes match.
_Stop and shake out your hand when your fingertips hurt._

The same check on the B string, with no drone. Play the ringed {{1}}, then bend the ringed {{b7}} two frets under it until it sounds the same.
Practice until the bend stops on the note without you playing the fretted one first.

Press Play below to start the metronome. Bend {{b7}} up to {{1}} again and hold it, then let the string down a little and push it back up, once on every click.
The top of each push is the note itself: vibrato on a bend dips under the note and comes back to it.

Press Play below to start the backing track, a 12-bar blues in {{=key}} minor. Improvise in the position, and end each phrase on one of the two bends, held with vibrato.
If a bend sounds sour against the backing track, play the fretted note and bend up to it again.
{{?key}}In another key the position sits on other frets, and the two bends are still {{4}} up to {{5}} on the G string and {{b7}} up to {{1}} on the B string.
